chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Sharif ibn Sabiq, from Al-Fadl ibn Abi Qurra, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Do you know what the greedy one (al-shahih) is?' I said, 'He is the miser (al-bakhil).' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Greed (al-shuh) is more severe than miserliness. Indeed, the miser is stingy with what is in his hand, but the greedy one is greedy for what is in the hands of people and for what is in his own hands, until he sees nothing in the hands of people but wishes it were his, whether by permissible or prohibited means, and he is not content with what Allah has granted him.'

key_terms.الشَّحِيحُ: The greedy one, one who is intensely desirous of others' wealth
key_terms.الشُّحُّ: Greed, a more severe form of stinginess involving covetousness
key_terms.الْبَخِيلُ: The miser, one who hoards his own wealth
key_terms.الْبُخْلُ: Miserliness, stinginess with one's own possessions

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between miserliness and greed in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) elucidates the spiritual hierarchy of stinginess, distinguishing *al-bukhl* (hoarding one's own wealth) from *al-shuh* (a deeper, insatiable greed for others' possessions). This distinction highlights that while the miser is content with his own stockpile, the *shahih* suffers from a fundamental discontent with divine decree (*al-qada*), seeking to acquire all worldly wealth through both lawful and unlawful means. This concept is central to Shia ethical teachings on purifying the heart from the love of the world (*hub al-dunya*).
